content: The referral process for wheelchair provision by general practitioners (GPs) and therapists, as well as the services for powered wheelchair users, did not adequately address the needs of indoor powered wheelchair users, who represent approximately 1% of the population. A survey conducted among 17 Disability Service Centres (DSCs) revealed that only 47% of centres responded, and of these, only 13% provided a locally developed information sheet alongside the official Her Majesty’s Stationery Office (HMSO) leaflet and the manufacturer’s booklet on battery charging guidelines. Half of the centres issued only the Department of Health and Social Security (DHSS) leaflet, while 38% provided both the DHSS leaflet and the manufacturer’s booklet. Among 36 district wheelchair services in England and Wales, 64% responded to the survey. Of these, 17% had locally developed maintenance information sheets or booklets, and 9% provided these alongside the DHSS leaflet and the manufacturer’s booklet. Ten centres (43%) issued only the manufacturer’s booklet, 3 centres (13%) issued only the DHSS leaflet, and 26% provided both. The content and format of wheelchair service information materials require improvement, and the role of referring health practitioners needs to be strengthened. In 22 cases, referrals were made by medical professionals, in 14 cases by non-medical professionals, and in 9 cases by other individuals. Comprehensive wheelchair services were received by less than half of eligible members of the Croatian Paraplegic and Tetraplegic Alliance. Active occupational therapy interventions, using a checklist for safety, comfort, positioning, maneuverability, and transportation, showed variable impacts on adult manual wheelchair users. A pre-post study on wheelchair breakdowns found that brake handles were the most frequently repaired component, as they were not manufactured to specifications. Repairs were required on 83 wheelchairs at the second visit and 21 at the third visit. The adjustable wheelchair provided in the Center for International Rehabilitation (CIR) Whirlwind project had favorable outcomes, except for the brake handles, which required frequent repairs. A cohort study by Toro, Eke, and Pearlman (2016) reported that few participants self-reported the need for repairs, and the World Health Organization’s (WHO) 8-step wheelchair service provision model resulted in minimal repair needs. Another study by Beaumont-White and Ham (1997) found that 26% of users contacted an approved repairer for issues, while 48% contacted the service directly. Most users (85%) initially checked their wheelchairs for faults themselves. Over a 12-month period, 30% of users reported no repairs, while the remainder had one (30%), two or three (30%), or more (10%) repairs. The referral process for powered wheelchair services requires review and improvement to better meet user needs. A mixed-methods study by D’Innocenzo et al. found that 8% of participants reported wheelchair malfunctions within 3 to 6 months, with common issues including wheel lock malfunctions and bearing problems. Repairs often involved tire replacements and fixing broken wheels. Poor repair services and the lack of a loan system for backup wheelchairs during repairs were significant concerns for users, as highlighted in the Irish wheelchair services study. A cohort study on wheelchair abandonment by Verza et al. and a cross-sectional study by Salatino et al. emphasized the importance of providing wheelchairs suited to the user’s environment and needs to prevent abandonment. A qualitative study by Williams et al. (2017) highlighted that inadequate spare parts and maintenance, coupled with environmental wear and tear, led to frequent wheelchair replacements. The WHO 2008 guidelines-based wheelchair service faced challenges in providing durable and suitable wheelchairs. A study by Divanoglou et al. (2019) using the Moorong Self-Efficacy Scale (MSES) found no significant changes in total scores, except for improvements in personal function after a 7-day active rehabilitation program for individuals with spinal cord injuries. Another study by Toro, Eke, and Pearlman (2016) using the WHO Quality of Life-BREF (WHOQOL-BREF) tool reported better environmental health outcomes for wheelchair recipients compared to those on waiting lists, with female recipients also reporting improved physical health. A mixed-methods study by Gowran et al. (2020) highlighted the importance of wheelchairs in enhancing freedom, independence, quality of life, and mental health. Participants reported improved societal participation and independence, with many contributing to household activities. A quasi-experimental study by Hoenig et al. found no significant differences in wheelchair confidence between users receiving expert rehabilitation services and those receiving usual care. A randomized controlled trial by Trefler et al. (2010) demonstrated that elderly individuals in institutional settings benefited from individually fitted manual wheelchair systems, which improved mobility, reach, quality of life, and satisfaction with technology. A mixed-methods study by Di Marco et al. (2003) emphasized the importance of documenting goals and objectives in wheelchair prescription to foster a common understanding among staff and improve service delivery practices. Overall, the studies underscore the need for improved wheelchair services, including better repair systems, user-centered designs, and comprehensive training for service providers. Enhanced policies, such as long-term wheelchair loans and stricter review processes, have shown success in addressing challenges and reducing costs.
